As I have already said today, someone from the Vlasenica platoon was late or too late to go to Srebrenica and this was a sort of punishment meted out to that soldier. His punishment was that he had to kill that Muslim. I stand by my statement that on the next day Pelemis told that person and another soldier to go and kill that individual, but I'm also saying that Pecanac was involved in that affair before Pelemis issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Who is Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who he was. I know he was in our unit, and I believe he was below Colonel Salapura of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just clarify one thing having to do with the 12th, Your Excellency, and the wounding, or rather, injuries that Pelemis sustained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you let us know the specific question you are going -- you wish to put before putting that to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to ask whether it is correct that on the way back to Vlasenica Pelemis was injured because there was an overturned APC and whether he was -- whether he had gone to the headquarters or the base or to the hospital. Because as far as we know, Pelemis was taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he answered -- he testified to that. Yes, Mr. Erdemovic, could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we arrived in Dragasevac at the base on the 12th, on the night of the 12th, Pelemis was not there. As I've already said, Major Pecanac was there, and then we heard of the incident with Pelemis, Dragan Koljivrat and Mladen, that they were in the overturned APC, the UN APC. Koljivrat was killed in that accident, Mladen was in a critical condition, and Pelemis - and I saw him the next day - only had a Band-Aid on his head. So I can't really say what happened with Pelemis on that particular night, but this is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Erdemovic. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just before the next witness comes in, I think the Court should give him a caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for five minutes, just to prepare for the next witness. --- Break taken at 11.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Good morning to you, General Milovanovic. By now you must be well aware of this, but before you start giving evidence I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now is go through your background a little bit, and then after we do that, start talking about the early days of the Main Staff of the VRS in 1992. But first, some of your background. Could you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Manojlo Milovanovic. I was born on the 21st of November, 1943, in Laminci village, Gradiska municipality, Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go briefly through your military career, which is quite a long one. So could you tell us briefly when you first began your career in the military and take us up through the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you could just take us briefly step by step through the positions you held.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The school for non-commissioned officer I completed from 1959 through 1961 in Banja Luka artillery. I was a sergeant and I was transferred to Benkovac in Zadar to serve there, where I remained for 14 months. And I then applied and was enrolled at the land forces academy, military academy, in Belgrade, which I attended from October 1962 through September 1966, when I was promoted to active-duty officer of the JNA. My first post was in Banja Luka from 1966 up until 1975. I was the commander of a tank platoon, commander of a tank company, a commander of the reconnaissance -- of a reconnaissance company, commander of a company in the reserve officers school for armoured assets. I was the chief of the reserve school for reserve officers in Banja Luka. At that time I also completed the political school of the JNA, and then in 1975, I applied for and was enrolled in the higher military academy in Belgrade. I believe that today it is called General Staff School for Tactics. I completed the academy in 1997 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- where -- from where I was transferred to Prilep in Macedonia. For four years I was in the Prilep garrison as the commander of an armoured battalion. And then in 1981, there was some sort of reorganisation within the JNA and I was transferred from Prilep to Titov Veles garrison, also in Macedonia, where I was an operative in the command of the 212th Motorised Brigade. I remained in that post until 1986 when I was assigned to the war college in Belgrade or the operations school, which I completed in 1987. And then I was again posted as the commander of the 212th Motorised Brigade in the Titov Veles garrison. I remained in that post until the 30th of January, 1989, when I was transferred to the Skopje garrison, to the command of the 3rd Army District as an operative in the army command. I was still there when Yugoslavia broke up and the JNA began to withdraw from Slovenia, Croatia, and Macedonia. When the withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia began, I was appointed as the chief of the operations and training sector as a general. It was a post for generals. As part of the withdrawal of the -- or during the withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia, I was appointed as the point man for pulling out the combat assets of the JNA, in other words, the personnel, materiel, ammunition, and all other combat assets of the JNA. And there was only one condition: To avoid starting a war in Macedonia. This was completed by the 9th of March, 1992, when together with the 3rd Army command I moved to the Nis garrison, where the army command was headquartered. I remained at the Nis garrison for five weeks, where I was the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army. This was in addition to my regular duties. On the 8th of May, 1992, I received two decrees from the Supreme Command of the armed forces of what was still the rump SFRY. According to one of the decrees, which was dated the 25th of April, 1992, I was promoted to the rank of major-general. And the other decree, which was dated the 26th of April of the same year, ordered my transfer to the Sarajevo garrison, to the 2nd District command as the chief of operations and training in the army command. In other words, that was the same post that I had in the 3rd Army. The dead-line for the implementation of the second decree in Belgrade was the 12th of May, 1992. I reported to the personnel administration of the General Staff of the JNA. It was still the JNA. I was told then that because of the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo and the losses suffered by the command of the 2nd Army Military District in Sarajevo, that my transfer was thereby altered. And instead of becoming the chief of operations at training, I was appointed the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District. And General Ratko Mladic was appointed commander of the 2nd Military District, who was replacing General Milorad Kukanjac, who was replaced by the General Staff because of the events in the Dobrovoljacka Street with the JNA and so on. I was told then that a decision had been made within the -- what was still SFRY that a contingent of the JNA should be withdrawn from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Serbia and Montenegro by the 19th of May, 1992. I protested with the chief of personnel, General Gojko Krstic, and I asked why I was going to Sarajevo. Because if the JNA was withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was there for me to do there? I was told that I should get on a helicopter, fly to Bosnia, where General Ratko Mladic would explain to me what it was that I was expected to do. I did so. I landed at around 11.00 p.m. on a field some 9 kilometres to the north-east of Han Pijesak. The area was called Crna Rijeka. General Mladic was not at the post, nor was General Kukanjac there because on that day he was supposed to leave Bosnia. Nor was another general there, I can't recall his name right now, but he was the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District and I was supposed to -- he was supposed to hand-over his duties to me. General Mladic came sometime in the evening hours on the 11th of May. He flew over from Herzegovina by helicopter, and from the Heliodrom up to the barracks where we would be stationed in the following five years, we walked some 45 minutes to an hour which is a distance of some 50 metres. And during this time he explained to me what it was that we could expect. As we entered the barracks, we found two other generals there, Djordje Djukic and Milan Gvero, and eight other men who were at the colonel or the lieutenant-colonel level. Mladic then explained or described the procedure in the establishment of the VRS as the seventh armed force that was to be established in the area of the former SFRY. On the next day there was supposed to be a meeting and it was held, the 16th Session of the People's Assembly of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina in Banja Luka, when the decision was made that Republika Srpska was going to establish the VRS. The Assembly appointed General Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff and authorised him to appoint his assistants, who would then be appointed by the president of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me stop you right there because we're now going into some other topics that I was going to cover. But just before we move on, what was your position from May 1992, let's say 12th, 13th of May, 1992, on, into 1996?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Main Staff of the VRS and at the same time the deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we move on I wanted to ask you a couple more -- just a couple more questions which relate to the topic you started telling us about, the 11th of May, when you met with General Mladic and some other officers in Crna Rijeka. Before that, when did you first meet Ratko Mladic? If you can tell us when you first got to know the man.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I met Major Ratko Mladic in April 1981 in Titov Veles garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just how would you characterise your relationship with him from that point until May 1992? As colleagues? Friends? Or how well you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, Ratko Mladic was an officer -- a trainings officer in the 3rd Army command and I was an operations officer in that command within the 212th Motorised Brigade. One day an inspection arrived from the army headquarters, and one of the inspectors was Major Ratko Mladic. When an inspection comes to a -- to your unit from a superior command - and this was the second as -- higher superior command - usually a commander would appoint an officer from their own command who would be escorting each one of those inspectors from the supreme -- higher command. Mladic was inspecting the situation with training and guidance. And of course because this was within my remit, I was assigned to be the escort for Major Mladic. He first inspected the physical fitness of a company and the discipline of rope climbing. One of the privates did not do the job well, he was unable to climb that rope all the way up. And Mladic then began criticising the company commander, that he did not properly train his men. And he concluded his story with the following words, and I'll give you an approximation. Since you, lieutenant, were unable to train your private properly, Major Milovanovic will now demonstrate how that is done properly, rope climbing, in other words. On that day -- a few days earlier I had just left the hospital. I had some health issue. And, well, for one, I wasn't even sure that I would be able to climb that rope. And I then said, "Well, Major, sir, since you are a superior officer and I'm afraid that I might make a mistake while showing this private -- these privates how to do it, perhaps the best thing would be for you to show them how to do it." For about 30 seconds he stared at me like a snake trying to hypnotise a frog. And then he smiled and then when the analysis -- when this inspection was completed, he, surprisingly, commended the work done there in the 212th Brigade. And to me, he turned to me and said, "The two of us will be able to co-operate well in the future." And he embraced me. I knew him from that time on. I remained in the brigade, but he went from the brigade command to Ohrid where he was the commander of an infantry regiment. And I heard from other colleagues that he was very capable and that he trained that regiment very well and very soon, that he accomplished very good results. So all the stories about General Mladic were very positive. It so happened that we were assigned to the war college together, both of us. We were in the same class. So for a whole year we travelled to Belgrade -- from Macedonia to Belgrade and back every day. Now, this school involves two phases of training. The first training is in the open and then the second phase of the training is in Belgrade in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, if I can interrupt, General. When was that that you're talking about now, when you went to -- you worked together at the school in Belgrade for a whole year and travelled together, what year was that if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that. That was 1986 through 1987. October 1986 through October 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you met in -- on May 11, 1992, was the relationship then one of mutual respect; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you've interrupted me just when I was going to describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- when it was that we worked together well and when we didn't. I said that on the 13th of January we were both transferred to the command of the 3rd Army. At that time Lieutenant-Colonel Ratko Mladic and Lieutenant-Colonel Manojlo Milovanovic, that's what we were. Now, Ratko Mladic was appointed chief of training in the army command and I was appointed chief of the operations department in the same command. These functions by rank and other requirements, training and years of service and so on, are similar. However, Mladic was in charge of training and I was in charge of combat-readiness of that same 3rd Army. However, the level of training and fitness of the army is, in fact, part of combat-readiness. In other words, Mladic's post was more dependent on mine than the other way around. We were -- both our departments were in charge, among other things, of training command officers and carrying out exercises within the command. We were in charge of defining the combat tasks. And it turned out that we had similar ideas but we had different ideas on how to accomplish them. And this is where our first differences began. And it went so far that the Chief of Staff or the chief of the army command had to intervene, and this is where there was this first misunderstanding between us. The chief of the army staff, as the staff officer, supported me because I was a staff officer as well; whereas Zivota Avramovic supported Mladic because Mladic had a longer experience as a commander. And fortunately, the staff commander was the one who decided in this -- on this issue so that I was in a better position there. Once this was resolved, we had no more issues between us. Soon after that there were -- there was -- there were tensions rising in Kosovo and the JNA was supposed to demonstrate, enforce, and implement a truce to place under control these protesters. We were then working together. He was in charge of training and I was in charge of determining how much time they would spend where. So we had -- we worked well together. In 1990, General Mladic -- or rather, then Colonel Mladic was transferred to Pristina, to the 52nd Corps, known as the Kosovo Corps. He became assistant corps commander for logistics. This was a surprise, both for him and for all of us who were around him. Mladic was a command officer who had a future, and then all of a sudden he was appointed assistant commander for logistics. Then we parted, he went to Kosovo, and then from Kosovo in 1991 he was transferred to Knin as an operations officer, to the Knin Corps, the 9th Corps of the JNA, and then he continued his career in that Knin Corps including the beginning of war operations between JNA forces in Dalmatia and the Croatian paramilitaries, the Green Berets. So while he was in Knin, Mladic very soon from an operations officer became commander of the corps in the beginning of 1992. His tour in Knin was cut short by this decree on his transfer to Sarajevo. On that 11th of May, when he said to me roughly what would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he came by helicopter from Herzegovina because the JNA was withdrawing. General Perisic was commander of the Bileca Corps of the JNA, and I assumed, travelling by helicopter, that I would probably be taking this Herzegovina Corps over from Perisic. And when Mladic landed, I told him to tell the helicopter pilot not to turn the helicopter off because I would be going to Bileca. However, he said, "You're not going anywhere. You're going to stay here and you're going to be chief of the Main Staff after the decision is taken by the Assembly tomorrow and you're going to be my deputy." So from them I found out that the pattern would be as follows: He would be the commander. However, from that evening onwards, we behaved as if we did not know who the commander would be until the decision was actually made by the Assembly. When I heard that I would be his deputy, I remembered a bit all the things that happened in Macedonia and Skopje. I did not ask him then, I asked him about six months later, "How did you find me to be your deputy commander." He said to me in the presence of Patriarch Pavle, the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church, he said, "You ignite your car in the third gear, I anything ignite mine in the first gear, and as a tank operator you know that the second gear works best." During the war we did not clash much -- well, since I was his assistant commander for combat operations, as Chief of Staff I strove for my ideas, but once he would make the decision, then he did not have a more passionate executor of his decisions than I was. So that is what I have to say about Mladic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I want to talk about the 12th of May, 1992, just before the break. You started speaking about that, the 16th Assembly Session. Now, did you attend that session personally?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did any officers who were with you and with General Mladic on the 11th of July, who would later become members of the Main Staff, did they go to Banja Luka for the 12th May session?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning after that night session of ours, General Mladic went to Banja Luka, as did General Gvero, General Djukic, and Colonel Tolimir. I'm sure that those people went there. They left me in Crna Rijeka to organise, during the Assembly session, the work of the Main Staff and to work out a schematic or a system of organisation for the future army so that once they were back we could work this out. I stayed there throughout the 12th; however, I did not only work on the organisation of the Main Staff but also on communications with subordinates and everything else that is required of a staff. But already in the morning I started receiving reports from the field, first from the 4th Corps of the JNA, the Sarajevo Corps; and then from all units, all units on the outskirts that were in contact with the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia and with paramilitaries of the Muslim-Croat coalition, that's the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, the Croatian defence forces, or the HOS as they were called, and I don't know, all other paramilitaries. So wherever there were conflicts, commanders by some inertia called Crna Rijeka because according to the war plan that was the command post of the 2nd Military District or the 2nd Army in war time. So people by way of inertia used these communications that were still functioning so they called me. Since the JNA was involved in the conflict predominantly, or rather, it was withdrawing, it was defending itself, I could not make any decisions in relation to them. I could only help them establish a column, leave, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: So I was not in Banja Luka on that day, the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And so -- just so if I understand, in that case, the communications which had formally been in place were still functioning so that, for instance, if General Talic, for example, in the 5th Corps had needed to, he could contact you at the Main Staff on the 12th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, I rearranged the command desk, if you will, so that I could receive information from all the existing five corps and the command of the air force as the sixth one, so that I could have button communications, as we call it in the army. I directly press a button at that desk, I don't have to go through a secretary or whoever. So until nightfall on that day, the 12th of May, until they return from Banja Luka, I could directly get in touch with all the units that would be resubordinated to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me just ask you: When did General Mladic and Generals Gvero and the other officers who'd attended the 16th Assembly Session, when did they return to Crna Rijeka, to the Main Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when they returned, Generals Djukic and Gvero and Colonel Tolimir. I know that Mladic returned at some point when it got dark. Now, whether they stayed in some other units along the way or whether they arrived in a separate vehicle -- at any rate, I do not remember when these three men arrived at the Main Staff. However, on the morning of the 13th, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on the morning of the 13th, had -- General Mladic had now been officially appointed commander of the Main Staff. When was it that the Main Staff became able to function as a Main Staff, if you understand my question? When were things really kind of up and running for the Main Staff that you'd been working on, on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that 12th of May, as far as the army was concerned, only one thing had been resolved: The Assembly had decided who the commander of the army of the Main Staff would be. Now practically he had some work to do over a few days to establish the Main Staff because there happened to be only 12 of us there. However, according to the establishment that we had worked out, the Main Staff was supposed to involve over 100 men. Now, this is another story all together, but the Main Staff could start functioning immediately on the morning of the 13th of May, that is to say, it could start, exist, legally. During the previous two nights, we were sort of illegal because we were still in the stage of being established. So practically, the Main Staff started operating on the 13th of May. And then comes the period of the establishment of the armies and re-establishing the Territorial Defence units that we found there, then the re-structuring of JNA units, those that would remain in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were quite a few garrisons, Muslims, Croats, Slovenes, Albanians, Macedonians left these units, so there would be a few Serbs here and there. For example, in the 4th Artillery Regiment all the combat equipment was left there, we kept it, that is. We had about ten Serbs who had served in that regiment previously, so we had to train or train additionally extra people very fast, because it's no use having a howitzer if you don't have someone who knows how to operate it. So the Army of Republika Srpska, as I reported to the supreme commander, only on the 23rd of June was fully ready on the basis of the concept itself and on the basis of the Law on Defence. However, we were already finishing the first operation of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that was establishing a corridor through Semberija in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But let me -- thank you, General. And we'll get to some of those topics. I think it's time for a break, if I'm right. But let me ask you - if I may, Your Honours - one question before the break. You just said that on the 23rd of June -- excuse me. You said that you reported to the supreme commander that only on the 23rd of June everything was fully ready. Who was the supreme commander? Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The supreme commander was the president of the republic, the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, just a couple more questions on the Main Staff. We said that the commander of the VRS Main Staff was General Mladic. You were the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff and General Mladic's deputy commander. And is it right that that Main Staff had seven different sectors?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just for -- as of July 1995, if you could just run through the seven sectors for me, not necessarily explaining all of their duties and roles, but who was in charge, chief or assistant commander, for the different sectors, please?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first was the staff sector, and I headed that particular one. It had an operations administration headed by General Miletic and it had a training administration and the heads changed. Colonel Prstojevic, Colonel Obradovic at the time, so people changed. Then the next sector is the sector for moral guidance headed by General Gvero. Then the sector for logistics, or rather, rear services, that's what we called it, and it was headed by General Djukic. Then the security and intelligence sector that was headed by General Tolimir. Then the sector for administration, mobilisation, and personnel affairs, it was General Petar Skrbic that headed that sector. Then the financial sector -- actually, it's not a sector. It's an administration that was headed by General Stevo Tomic. And we had an administration for the air force and anti-aircraft defence headed by General Jovo Maric. I don't know if I've omitted to mention someone perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, thank you. And if you could just tell us quickly what the 65th Protection Regiment was and who headed that regiment?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 65th Protection Regiment, the motorised regiment, is the unit that provided immediate security to the Main Staff. The head of that regiment from the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska up until the end of the war was at first captain first class - at the end he became a colonel - so it was Milomir Savic, Colonel Milomir Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was there also a department for civil affairs? I'm not sure if you mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a separate -- or rather, there wasn't a separate administration. This work was done for -- by people from the sector for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs, headed by General Gvero, Milan Gvero. People changed there. There were desk officers, if you will. There was co-operation with humanitarian aid organisations, and then in Tolimir's sector, there were desk officers for co-operation with UNPROFOR. And it was only at some point towards the end of the war that we established an administration for relations with foreign armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember who was the head of that administration?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, when this administration was established, but then that was after the Dayton Agreement, I think it was headed by then-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember a man -- a Colonel Milos Djurdjic, did he have a role in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milos Djurdjic, he's deceased now. His role was one of co-ordination, co-ordination between representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska with representatives of UNPROFOR and the UNHCR, and this had to do with humanitarian aid supplies. Practically he was the man from the Main Staff who worked with that commission of Republika Srpska for providing humanitarian aid, and it was headed by the vice-president of the republic, Nikola Koljevic. The establishment of that commission considerably facilitated the work of the Main Staff, or rather, it disburdened the Main Staff. Because until then it was the Main Staff that made decisions in terms of whether they would allow convoys or not. However, this commission took over that role. So we, or the army, received the task of checking these convoys, ensuring their safe passage, and allowing their entry at these check-points into the places where the aid was needed, that is to say, the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll talk about that a little bit later, that commission. And the structure we've -- you've helped describe to us with the different sectors, was that essentially the same structure throughout the war, from May through July 1995 and later? Although the people would have changed of course, some of the personnel.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The structure itself did not change. As you said, it was the personnel, the people, who changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked just before the break about how you reported to the supreme commander in June of 1992 and that that was Radovan Karadzic, the president. General Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff. As of 13th of May, 1992, who was General Mladic's direct superior?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand that. Who was General Mladic's superior? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Who was above General Mladic in the command chain?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The one and only superior of General Ratko Mladic was Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is something you've talked about in your interviews. Was Dr. Radovan Karadzic the president -- the commander, excuse me, of the army or of the armed forces of Republika Srpska? And could you tell us what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Radovan Karadzic was the supreme commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. That means the following -- the organisation of the armed forces is the following: The army of Republika Srpska, the police of Republika Srpska, and the civil protection of Republika Srpska. The difference lies in the following: Karadzic as the supreme commander of the armed forces does not command the army or the police or the civilian protection directly. Rather, he does that through Ratko Mladic, he commands the army. Through the Ministry of the Interior, he commands the police. And through the chief or commander - I don't even know what the name of the position was - through the man who was in charge of civilian protection, he commands the civilian protection. Now I'm going to attack President Karadzic's advisors immediately. For example, in the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, it says that President Karadzic is the supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. This made him directly responsible for the actions of the military; however, he was not directly responsible. He was indirectly responsible through Ratko Mladic, or rather, through the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is what his advisors allowed. They allowed that kind of sentence to be included in the Law on the Army and also in many, many other documents it says "supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska." No. He was the supreme commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just since you brought up the Law of the Army, let's take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's P02603. And could I have English page 24 and the Serbian language page 17. And I hope we have a legible version of the Serbian because -- yes, we do. No, we don't. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought we had a better version uploaded. I'll come back to this topic since the Serbian's not visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on now, General, again talking about the situation in, as you saw it, in May 1992 at the beginning. You described how you worked on -- worked on the communications and getting the Main Staff ready on 12 May. What was the situation regarding armed forces at that time that were defending the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? In other words, when you were setting up the Main Staff, what armed forces were there on the Serbian side, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the Main Staff was established, in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was the Yugoslav People's Army, which was withdrawing. And through combat, it engaged the Muslim paramilitary forces because they would seize their technical equipment and kill their personnel. On the Serb side, there were only organised units of the Territorial Defence which came into being after the territorial units of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina were replenished, or rather, the personnel was strengthened because the Muslims and the Croats had left and they all had weapons that they held at their homes. This was done in municipalities which were bordering on, let's say, the states of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then in the border areas of those territories, Serb territories that had already been rounded off. And I believe that that evening there was a fact provided by General Mladic that there were some 85.000 to 90.000 armed men on the territory of Republika Srpska who should now be organised into military units. And then in the territory of Republika Srpska there was several units, several paramilitary units of Serb composition, Serb ethnicity, such as Arkan's men, the Panthers of Mauzer, they operated in Bijeljina and its surroundings. And there was several groups in Sarajevo, Aleksic's Chetniks, Vaska's Chetniks, and others. I can't recall them all. In the territory that was under the control of the Croat-Muslim coalition there were still paramilitary units in existence, the Patriotic League that had been established in late 1990; the Green Berets, they were established sometime in 1991; the Croatian Defence Forces, the HOS, I'm not sure when they were established; and there was also the regular army of the state of Croatia which already by late 1991 and especially in March 1992 - in other words, before Bosnia and Herzegovina were internationally recognised - were active and organised operations in the areas of Brod, in the Sava River valley, the Neretva valley, western Herzegovina, the surroundings of Kupres, and for a large part Central Bosnia. Throughout the war, the state of Croatia had anywhere between 12 to 15 brigade commands which were part of the regular Croatian army which numbered between 35.000 to 50.000 troops. And I recently learned that in Operation Storm in June, July, and August 1995, that number even reached some 75.000 men. Of the armed groups in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or armed forces, there was also the UNPROFOR, as the peacekeepers of the UN; and after April 11, 1994, the NATO also became present and they -- as the enemy of the VRS and they engaged the Serbian side in Gorazde and also in a bombing campaign which went on from August through September 1995. So this was this whole conglomerate of various armed forces that were present on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when the Assembly session adopted that decision. On the 4th of April, 1992, in other words, almost a month and a week before the Army of Republika Srpska was established, they implemented mobilisation. And I have to stress one other thing. In this whole mess, armed mess, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was an agreement that was reached between the then-leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina - in other words, before Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared independent on the 6th of April, 1992 - and the leadership of the now already-rump SFRY, a decision to the effect that the JNA would remain in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the following five years, which would mean up until 1997. The expectation being that by that time, a peaceful resolution, political resolution, would be reached for all these multi-ethnic conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In those five years the JNA was supposed to equally defend the interests of all three major ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in other words, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. Because in early April, the Muslim-Croat coalition began attacking members of the JNA and the Serbs saw members of the JNA as their protectors so they did not attack them, it appeared as though the JNA had actually engaged in hostilities the coalition, the Muslim-Croat coalition, which is not true. Now, this topic as to who fought whom in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that would be a very broad topic and I think I can't go into that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just assist with the transcript. On page 69 on line 2 after General Milovanovic said even before Bosnia and Herzegovina was internationally recognised, the Croatian army launched an aggression or committed an aggression against the Bosnia and Herzegovina of AVNOJ, A-V-N-O-J, and I do understand why the interpreters did not get this because they don't know what AVNOJ is. And this did not make it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The reporters will take a look into that. Yes, let us continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You spoke about the 80- to 90.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but, General, can you confirm what Mr. Karadzic said about AVNOJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is -- that stands for Anti-Fascist Council of the National Liberation of Yugoslavia. That was a system of government that was established in 1943 at the second session of this AVNOJ in Jajce when, for all practical purposes, the Second Yugoslavia was established. The international community then took those borders as the legitimate borders, and whoever encroached on those borders, for instance, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would be treated as an aggressor against Bosnia and Herzegovina. My apologies, I have to add one more thing. In the first half of the war up until 1994, the second half of 1994, the Muslim-Croat coalition never referred to us as the enemy; rather, they referred to us as the aggressor. Serbia was referred to as the aggressor, and as for us Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were referred to as Serb Chetnik aggressors. Of course it was impossible for us to commit aggression against our own state because under international law, aggression is when the troops of one state enter the territory of another state. So Bosnia and Herzegovina was an AVNOJ whole. We had not come from Iceland to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor did the Serbia armed forces cross the Drina River. It was only in the second half of 1994 that they began referring to us the way we referred to them, in other words, the enemy. Up until then they only referred to us as "the aggressor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about how at the time the Main Staff was formed, that General Mladic had said there were 85- to 90.000 men or thereabouts who needed to be brought into the VRS, into that command. Can you tell us, in April/May, what was the role of the Serbian side Crisis Staffs in relation to armed men in the territory? Municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be as brief as possible. After the Patriotic League was established, and the Green Berets and the HOS, and the decision of the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was taken, that the JNA should withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina remained without any protection. We were the only ones who did not have any armed force; in other words, an army. Now, the leadership of the republic then proceeded to self-organise the people. And as I've already said, by strengthening the Territorial Defence units that already existed, they began organising them as units in those municipalities where Serbs were in the majority. Territorial Defence members had uniforms and weapons even before the break-out of the war and they held them at home. Now, since most of these units were municipal in character, the organisation of the Territorial Defence of the SFRY was as follows. There was a staff of Territorial Defence at the republic level, and then at the municipal level, there were municipal staffs of Territorial Defence that commanded these municipal TO units. The Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina probably established Crisis Staffs. These were groups of men and for the most parts the Crisis Staffs comprised presidents of municipalities, the commissioners of the SDS, the ruling party, and then the chiefs of police. In some places they were called commanders and in others chiefs of police. Then there were also prominent people from that particular municipality. Now, their task was to supply -- to provide supplies for these men in the brigades, the local brigades, to provide clothing, food, arms for those who did not have any weapons. And they elected to go by the system of - I would call it - readiness for defence. For instance, if there was a raid on a Serb village or hamlet, the number of men who were members of the brigade would be assigned to defend that village, that particular village. So that was one of the main tasks of the brigade headquarters, to actually create these brigades as light infantry brigades, infantry brigades in other words, to organise them into corps. There would be an operational corps, a strategic -- and then there were operational corps, strategic corps, Main Staff, and then the Supreme Command. I don't know if I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And if you could -- just let me ask you briefly. In the beginning, in the period after the establishment of the Main Staff of the VRS, were there any conflicts or difficulties with the municipal Crisis Staffs over who would command these local units and how they would be integrated into the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff expected that there might be possible problems, and during that same night, on the eve of that Assembly session, one of the conclusions that we adopted was that the Crisis Staffs should be excluded from the system of command. We wanted to bypass the military command -- the chain of command. It is true that these Crisis Staffs organised these brigades in municipalities, that they armed them, equipped them, that they provided personnel for those units. However, we did not give them the authority to command those units. That right was exclusively within the remit of the military. This is how we drafted this on the 11th and 12th of May. The order was issued on the 20th of June. It was obligatory for both the Crisis Staffs and the paramilitaries, although I think you will have more questions for me about paramilitaries so I won't dwell too much on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you now, since we started talking about paramilitaries a bit. Were you aware of Arkan's activities in Bijeljina in 1992 in March/April? Did you see that on television or learn about what was going on in Bijeljina with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I heard about Arkan when I arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was then concerned with not provoking a war in Macedonia. I heard over the television about certain volunteer units, detachments, that were being formed mostly in the territory of Serbia. They were being infiltrated into Kosovo, the northern borders of Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were detachments with fancy names that belonged to former -- that had the names of former Serbian warlords, Stevan Sindjelic, for example, who was present in Montenegro [as interpreted] and then was driven out. I know that the Supreme Command of the armed forces was still the SFRY. In 1990, in June, I think, it took the decision according to which all paramilitary formations in the territory of the SFRY should be disarmed. And the TO units, Territorial Defence units, throughout the territory of the former SFRY should return weapons to the military warehouses. Some obeyed, some didn't. On the whole, I know that Arkan's group - I think their name was the Tigers - didn't hand in their weapons, they didn't disarm. Later I found out about what they had done in the surroundings of Bijeljina. I found out much about them after the war thanks to you, or rather, to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now that you know, what is your view of what Arkan and his Tigers, what their activity was in Bijeljina in 1992? What's your personal view of what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to the part that concerns the Main Staff. On that evening, amongst other things, we also adopted the decision according to which commanders of paramilitary formations should be called to have a conversation with us and we should set conditions for them. First of all, they were to enter the structure of the future VRS. They should be placed under the Main Staff command. Those who refused to be placed under the VRS command were to be disbanded and were to leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since most of them were from Serbia, they were to return to Serbia and Montenegro. Those who refused to do that, who didn't want to be placed under our command and who didn't want to be disbanded were threatened with being physically removed by us. After that ultimatum had been issued, we also issued an order to that effect, which I have already mentioned. The date of the order is the 28th of June, 1992. And then it was stated that the VRS should go into action. Those were the regulations. Arkan then left Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was someone called Captain Dragan whom we drove out in a cheap manner, or rather, he received a task he couldn't carry out. We drove him out under the pretext that we didn't need such troops, that couldn't carry out their tasks. Mauzer, together with his Panthers, placed himself under the Main Staff's command initially, and later he was integrated into the Eastern Bosnia Corps. There was several small groups that remained around Sarajevo. They went by such and such names. They called themselves Chetniks of this kind or of that kind. They didn't bother the army. Sometimes they co-operated with us, took joint action with us. I think they were under the MUP. As to what Arkan did, I found out about this through the media. As to what he did in Bijeljina in 1992, I found out about that through the media and by following the proceedings here. So I didn't see anything of the events that are concerned. I know as much as you do, and you probably know more than I do. But I do know that he committed war crimes, and this was not within or on behalf of the state. So he was committing acts of private terrorism, private crimes, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just while we're still talking about Arkan, did you see or meet with Arkan in 1995 in the RS?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995 I met with Arkan in the presence of members of our Supreme Command, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, and I believe Biljana Plavsic too. I insisted on holding this meeting, and this was conveyed through the supreme commander, Mr. Karadzic. I think we spoke on the phone on three occasions. The meeting wasn't organised. I asked for the meeting because Arkan appeared in the combat zone for which I was responsible, and no one could enter that zone without my knowledge. And even the supreme commander abided by those rules. He would always inform me that he was coming or his representatives, mostly Biljana Plavsic would act in this manner. I found out about Arkan when he beat up my Colonel Svetozar Andric somewhere near Prijedor, and that colonel, Colonel Andric, before the war was the commander of the military police company in some sort of unit in Belgrade. And he arrested Arkan as an under-age delinquent. When this colonel reported to me and told me that he had been beaten up by Arkan, I first tried to joke about it with the colonel. And I said he was taking vengeance for the past. But later several other officers were beaten up and their heads were shaven, and I then tried to get the supreme commander to organise a meeting between Arkan and myself. I wanted to see who had called him or provided him with authorisation to go to the territory of Republika Srpska, but then he suddenly appeared with a combat formation in the vicinity of Kljuc. Recently I found out how this actually occurred. I met up with him in the evening. That was the third time I contacted the supreme commander about the matter. I met with him in the Banski Dvor building in Banja Luka. The conversation was not very dignified, it wasn't a conversation between officers. Initially -- in the end I gave him an ultimatum, and General Mladic and myself had agreed earlier to drive Arkan out of the territory of Republika Srpska. And on the following day he did leave the territory of Republika Srpska. I think that was on the 1st of September or perhaps the 30th or 31st of August, because on television, on the 2nd of September, I saw that he was escorted out of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you asked Arkan in the president -- in the presence of President Karadzic who had authorised him to come onto the territory of the RS and what he said?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we entered the premises where the conversation was to be held, General Momir Talic, the commander of the 1st Corps, and his Chief of Staff, Bosko Kelecevic, entered the premises, all the members of the Supreme Command whom I have already mentioned stood up. He remained sitting. I approached the seat where I was to sit down, and I said, "Get up." He got up. I was somewhat surprised. He first started speaking and he said, "I'm the son of a colonel and I know what the army is. A Serbian soldier needs to be given 25 strokes to the buttocks every day." I don't know what his exact words were. Perhaps I wasn't functioning properly then, but I said, "How do you, as a colonel's son who was rejected by his father when you were 14, how can you know more about the army than the three active-duty officers here?" And then there was some nonsense. For example, "It's easy for you, I have a 22-year-old wife who is pining after me." He was then 49 years old, something like that. I said, "My wife is 52 years old, so she can't even pine after me or suffer because of me. She leaps from trench to trench with me." I said, "Who ordered you to be present here?" And he said it was in accordance with the order issued by the Supreme Command. And I asked him whether he had the order and he said that he had. "Where is it? Give it to me." He said, "It's in the Bosna hotel." I said, "Go and fetch it." He got up, however, he sat down again very quickly and he mumbled something about having it or not having it, and then I came to the conclusion that he didn't have it. That is what he said, but I came to the conclusion that he didn't want to give it to me or couldn't. I then asked the supreme commander whether he had been issued with such an order, and Mr. Karadzic did not reply. He didn't say yes and he didn't say no. And then since I saw that any further conversation would be futile, I told him about the agreement reached between General Mladic and myself. We had agreed that I should go to Manjaca since they had a camp there. I'd drive out, disband the camp, and General Mladic on the way to Han Pijesak would go to Doboj, the village of Doboj, where he had the second part of that camp and Mladic would disband that camp. The meeting came to an end around 2.00, around 2.00 in the afternoon. When I arrived in the command, I saw a message from General Mladic, stating that I didn't have to do anything. They were already withdrawing. I contacted General Mladic, and he told me that he immediately acted on the basis of the ultimatum that I had issued. And that was the end of my story with Arkan. We clashed once again after the war in 1996. That was during the pre-election campaign. But I don't think that that clash has any importance for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me, if I can with Mr. Reid, play a quick video-clip. This is P02858. This video-clip should come up in front of you in a minute, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just stop here quickly at 00:14.8. Do you recognise where this is, General? Can you tell by that building?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The frozen image or the image that is very dark, it's the darkest image. I've seen this now about ten times. This is Bijeljina. I think the building in the background is the Municipal Assembly building in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if somebody can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It shouldn't be that dark --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- could you adjust the angle. If the usher could assist the General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While they were approaching, I saw Arkan quite clearly, but now I can just see the chin and the nose that are clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll just play it to the end of the clip now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General, is that clip we saw, you talked about after this incident you described in Banja Luka and the confrontation that Arkan left via Bijeljina soon after, is that what we saw just now?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is two days after that meeting of mine with Arkan at the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Before we move on from the paramilitaries, let me ask you this question: Coming back to Sarajevo, you mentioned that there was several groups in Sarajevo, Aleksic's Chetniks, Vaska's Chetniks. In Sarajevo did those paramilitary groups pose any problem to you in the Main Staff in terms of military command --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not mention a single name; Mr. Nicholls is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to check, Your Honour, but I think I heard some names. I'll take a quick look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to look any further. I did mention these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- I take Mr. Karadzic's word that it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 68, for the record, lines 18 and 19. Several groups in Sarajevo, Aleksic's Chetniks, Vaska's Chetniks, those are the ones I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember the question, did they cause problems for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not cause any problems for the Army of Republika Srpska. As a matter of fact, with me specifically they acted in concert - Vaska's Chetniks did - at Brgule; that involved expelling the Muslim forces from the Nisici plateau. Because on the 2nd of August, 1994, they slaughtered a few families and my task was to expel them, even from Mount Cemerno. As far as I remember -- or rather, as far as the supreme -- if the supreme commander remembers, it was called Brgule, this operation, it started on the 16th and we expelled them from Cemerno. That is when this unit of Vaska's Chetniks, as they were known, acted together with me, in co-ordination with me, a group of 40 or 50 men, well armed. And let me tell you, at the time they were good soldiers. When we finished that operation at Mount Cemerno, I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, sorry. One more thing. The General said that Muslim forces were expelled after they slaughtered some Serbian families, and that is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is reflected in the interpretation and the pace is too fast for court reporting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were slaughtered on St. Elijah's Day, the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you to the interpreters and reporters, we appreciate it for their contribution. Yes, back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now what I want to do is go and talk about some meetings between the VRS and the political leadership after the Main Staff began functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 01899, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, this is a document dated 26th of May, 1992, Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Main Staff. Could we show the -- you've seen this document before, I think, General, but could we just go to the second page in both versions. And do you see your name there in the Serbian version, and your position, your rank?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the document, if we go back to page 1, states: "At the meeting on 26 May 1992, the commanders and the Chief of Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH and the top political leadership of the republic discussed possible options for the Serbian Republic Army of organisational and establishment structure."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I have something done with the volume so that I can hear the interpreter better -- well, yes, now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you hear me? Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I hear you but you have to repeat your question because I had problems with my headphones and with my spectacles and with the volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No problem. I will repeat. The first sentence states: "At the meeting on 26 May 1992, the commanders and Chief of Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH and the top political leadership of the republic discussed possible options for the Serbian Republic Army of organisational and establishment structure." And then it continues. Can you just tell me who attended this meeting and briefly what it was about, what structures were -- what the purpose of this meeting was, which is quite shortly after the 16th Assembly Session on 12 May, two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who attended that meeting, I don't know. I mean, I cannot remember. But it says here that General Mladic and I were there. Also some other commanders, because it says commanders in the plural. Probably some of the corps commanders of the Sarajevo Corps or I don't know which corps. And there was a discussion on what kind of army we actually wanted. I see that I wrote this and signed it, and I said that I wanted fast mobile units. And I don't see anything controversial about that. Heaven forbid that I would have written that we wanted army that was not fast, that was slow, lackadaisical, with a lack of discipline, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just see if I can help you remember, just if this helps you. When we spoke a few weeks ago, I asked you about this document and asked who was present when it refers to top political leadership. And you said members of the Presidency, it was President Karadzic, Vice-Presidents Plavsic and Koljevic, President of the Assembly Krajisnik, and the Prime Minister Branko Djeric. For my colleagues, that's 65 ter 23628 is -- and that's the meeting on the 1st of February, 2012, on page 4. Does that help you remember at all who was present?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: A few weeks ago, as you said, I gave you an aide-memoire of mine regarding my meetings with President Karadzic. I think that this is what follows. This document is dated the 26th. And I think that what I wrote there was that we met on the 16th of May. My first contact with Mr. Karadzic was on the 14th of May, 1992, by telephone, when I conveyed to him what General Simunovic had told us, General Simunovic from the Army of Yugoslavia, who had come to free the imprisoned Serb officers, their families, cadets from military schools, and that involved an exchange that was carried out by giving the other side ammunition. I told President Karadzic about that on the telephone. The first time we ever met, President Karadzic and I, was on the 16th of May. All these persons were present, the persons that you mentioned just now. From the Main Staff I attended and so did Mladic. And also the meeting was attended by all presidents of municipalities of the Sarajevo region. I don't know whether you mean that we discussed that meeting on the 16th. As for the 26th, I stand by that. I wrote it, I signed it, fine. It has to do with the establishment of the corps. However, I cannot remember how, where, when we met on this 26th of June. I don't have that aide-memoire of mine. I'd have to look this up. There should be a record of a meeting with Mr. Karadzic then. Mr. Prosecutor, I don't see what is in dispute here. Do I recognise this document as my own or do I not recognise it as my own or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, there's nothing in dispute. There weren't any trick questions. I was simply trying to see if you remembered who was present at this meeting where it says "top presidential -- top political," excuse me, "leadership." And if you don't remember now, that's fine. I'll move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this as next exhibit from Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4492, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P01508, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, this is a 1st of June, 1992, Main Staff document that also has your name at the bottom. I just want you to take a look at this for a minute. This is also one that we talked about a few weeks ago. See if you remember it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I still have the document of the 26th of May, 1992, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number. 1518?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's right, General, it will come up in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. And could we blow it up, please, for the witness and scroll through it for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there's nothing in dispute about this document or whether it's valid or anything like that. It begins: "Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Main Staff of the army, a meeting of the political leadership of the republic and the military commanders is to be held in Pale on 3rd June 1992, Wednesday, at noon. In order to ensure timely preparations and arrival of the corps commanders and THE commander of the air force and AA defence, I hereby order ..." And then it continues and talks about briefings to be made. And then we see your name and the distribution list, that it was sent to the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the 1 and 2 KK Sarajevo Corps, East Bosnia Corps, et cetera. So first: Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember this document because on that day when this meeting was held, it was the first time that I was frightened ever in my life. First of all, I did not attend the meeting. Let's be clear on that. But I was in charge of organising the meeting and I regulated the transportation involved. The transportation was carried out by helicopter and at daybreak I was still in some bed when helicopters attacked. They were V-8s, and I think that someone was attacking the Main Staff, and that's why I remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just briefly, what was the purpose of the meeting and of the briefings which were going to be given?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was -- if you remember those earlier orders that we saw that discussed what needed to be done in the corps and what types of units we wanted, the corps commanders were tasked to report by the 27th of June what status they had in their areas, what kind of units, arms, and so on. So they had to report how they had implemented the order, I believe, of the 26th of May. And simply put, the other purpose was for the corps commanders to get to know each other and also for the supreme commander to meet their commander -- the commanders, the second in command, that level of command. It was just a working meeting, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm done with that document which is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to move on now, General, we've -- in the time we have left today and talk about the creation of the Supreme Command in November 1992. Can you tell us about that event and how it -- what it meant for the Main Staff. I know that you think that there was some mistakes made in the way that the Supreme Command was constituted. Can you tell us about that body.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On the 6th of December, 1992, General Djordje Djukic and Colonel Zdravko Tolimir returned to the Main Staff, in other words, the chief of the logistics department and the chief of the security and intelligence department. I don't know where General Mladic was at the time, but they were supposed to report to the superior officer who was present there on their visit to Pale. Among other things, they told me that work was being done to establish the Supreme Command and that part of that Supreme Command should be the president of the republic, the president of the Assembly - the popular Assembly - the president of the government, the prime minister, the minister of the interior, and the minister of defence. I asked whether General Mladic appeared anywhere on that list and they said no. From -- by looking at the list, I also noticed that the vice-president of the republic's name was also absent. When General Mladic returned - and I can't recall where he was - I told him, I briefed him on the reports of these two and then a debate opened on why there was no one there to represent the army, or rather, why General Mladic wasn't there. And it was surprising why the first and second vice-presidents of the republic weren't there, Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic. I don't know whether it was Mladic or whoever else who reported this to the Presidency, but at the first session of the Supreme Command, which was held on the 20th of December, 1992, I was invited as a member of the Main Staff to attend as an observer, as it were. I asked the Supreme Command the same question, I put the same question to them and President Karadzic said that the two of us would talk about this in private. I can't recall what was discussed at that Supreme Command session, but not waiting for this one-on-one meeting in his office, I tried to explain that an error had been made, that it was on error on organisation and establishment. Had General Mladic been a member of the Supreme Command, then the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, which was still incomplete at the time and not fully capable and not fully able to produce the documents that are supposed to come out from the Supreme Command, in other words, directives, mobilisation documents, and so on, army supplies, et cetera, a whole host of problems that they were supposed to deal with. In other words, by the fact that General Mladic was not a member of the Supreme Command, the Ministry of Defence would not be part of the Supreme Command. Had that happened, the Main Staff would have been the professional body that would advise the president, the Supreme Command, on the use of the army. The Muslims already had a staff of -- in the Supreme Command. All the other countries that fortunately never waged wars did have Supreme Commands -- did have staffs and Ministries of Defence would automatically become staffs of supreme -- of the Supreme Command. And if you look at history and all the socialist countries that existed at the time, Ministries of Defence were professionals. In Russia they were marshals, they were called marshals, and in our case it was generals. Ex officio, the minister of defence would be the first, the right hand of the Supreme Command. He would be the main boss in the army for issues that had to do with the army. So we could have just -- the Main Staff could immediately then be renamed to be called the General Staff. Now, a few days later there was a correction and we learned that the first and second vice-president did become members of the Supreme Command, but General Mladic was still not there. So now the Main Staff was put in a spot where they had to implement the orders of the Supreme Command, but because we were not part of the Supreme Command, the only connection between us and the Supreme Command would be the supreme commander, under the constitution. In other words, all other members of the Supreme Command were excluded from the chain of command. So, for instance, Momcilo Krajisnik would never issue any orders to the army; and if he ever did try, we would never act on it without informing the supreme commander. Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic as vice-presidents could not issue orders for the use of the army. However, whenever President Karadzic was absent from the theatre of war, when he was visiting abroad, he would leave behind Biljana Plavsic as his deputy. He had nothing against that, but simply put, there was an error in the organisation and establishment in setting up the chain of command within the army. True, that Supreme Command did not frequently bypass the Main Staff, which was a good thing, and it went on like that throughout the war. However, whenever military decisions had to be made, whenever decisions on the use of the army had to be made, we were invited as guests - either Mladic or me or other assistants - to these Supreme Command sessions. But we didn't have any voting rights. I do have to say that our proposals would usually be heeded, but all of this was done without the Main Staff, with bypassing the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again in the transcript I have to intervene, without the legal protection of the Main Staff, without the legal provisions for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to say this. The Main Staff did not have any legitimacy, any legal protection for their own decisions. In other words, it was not the Main Staff that was supposed to provide legal protection for anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And tomorrow we'll look at some minutes, one of -- one of the few we have of a meeting of the Supreme Command where you were present. And we can talk about the way it functioned then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm about to start a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can either go for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we shall adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, but you are aware of this, I take it, that you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand and this is the sixth time that I've been advised of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
